Gradually, through the practice of yoga, he united into one the divided / vital breaths named prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
Thus drawing it into the heart, holding it in all the joints, / and bringing it to the seat of Brahman, he firmly applied it to Brahman.
When he draws in the external breath and fills the body, / then that is to be known as inhalation (pūraka); now I shall explain exhalation (recaka).
And when the internal breath gradually departs outside, O king, / then that is to be known as exhalation; from retention arises kumbhaka.
When yogins know the twenty-five principles, / they are freed from all sins, even those committed in seven lifetimes.
The king said: / Which are the principles? Who is the embodied soul? Tell me what yogins ought to know. / How does one in whom the true nature of knowledge has arisen become united with yoga?
Īśvara said: / Primordial nature (prakṛti), and from that intellect (buddhi), then egoism (ahaṃkāra) arose; / from that the five subtle elements: such is the eightfold prakṛti.

17.18.m:
Know the five organs of perception and the five organs of action, / the mind as the eleventh, and the five gross elements;
This group of sixteen has been proclaimed at length in the Sāṃkhya. / These are twenty-four principles; the person (puruṣa) is the twenty-fifth.
He is called the embodied soul within the body, and he perceives the self. / They attain the supreme self, which is the twenty-sixth, beyond the twenty-five.
The varieties of postures and so forth are always to be known first. / When they see a light resembling the flame of a lamp within the heart,
Those yogins are declared by the wise to be ones in whom the true nature of knowledge has arisen. / First he wears away old age; diseases perish far away;
When the mass of all sins is exhausted, he subsequently encounters death. / No man in the world dies if the yogin knows it himself.
Then, closing the ten apertures, he releases the breaths. / Having exhausted merit and sin, the breaths of the yogins depart; / they attain the lordly power of the qualities such as lightness in the abode of Śiva.

17.18.m:
Through this yoga of meditation, a mortal beholds Bhava. / Everything conceived by the mind is attained through the vision of Bhava.
While the brahmin Vāmana remained thus in the presence of Bhava, / he then saw Nārada descended from the sky.
Vāmana said: / Great seer, is all well with you today? Whence have you come? / I bow to you, great seer; you are indeed Brahmā in the three worlds.
Nārada said: / I have arrived from the world of heaven. What well-being can I tell you of?
By the comings and goings of the sun, a day of Brahmā is completed. / At the end of the day night arises; in the night the deities perish.
What to say of the mortal world, where people die day by day? / The sky has become filled with smoke; the gods have gone to the house of Bali.
The seven seers, chaste disciples of Brahmā, have gone there; / Hāhā, Hūhū, and Tuṃbaru, and both Nārada and Parvata have gone.
The hosts of apsarases and gandharvas have arrived at Bali's palace. / A sacrifice to pacify portents is being performed by Bali himself.

I wish to go right there, to see the sacrifice at Bali's house. / Bali has performed nine hundred and ninety-nine sacrifices.
When this is completed, the entire realm will belong to the Daityas. / Some extraordinary vow has been undertaken by him in the sacrificial rite: / 'Whatever is personally asked for by the twice-born must be given by me.
Even if forbidden, it must be given by me; let my word be true! / Even myself, my wives, kingdom, and my beloved sons—
If requested, should I not give, let my sacrifice be in vain!' / Because of this statement of his, a great headache has arisen in me: / having made this vow, how will this sacrifice be completed?
I see no means of foiling it, though I wander through the three worlds. / Knowing you to be the destroyer of it, I have approached you.
Act now in such a way that the sacrifice is not completed.
Vāmana said: / Great seer, hear my words: what power is there in me? / Who am I, and why should I do this? The gods have gathered at the sacrifice,

The gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, consisting of the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas. / Thus Brahmā performs creation, and Hari preserves it;
Hara destroys the entire threefold world, together with the moving and unmoving. / Having set this in motion, the lords of gods sat on excellent seats / on the delightful peak of Kailāsa and took counsel with one another.
"Among the three, which god is superior? Which is the eldest? Which has more virtues?" / There was no fourth who knew; the three of them stood suddenly perplexed.
From them arose a blazing light that merged into one in the sky; / endowed with the measure of time, it revolved as the solar orb.
"I am the eldest!" "No, I am the eldest!"—thus a dispute arose between Hara and Brahmā. / As the two argued, out of their wrath I was born from the mouth, O Lord.
"Why, O god, do you not know what was spoken by Brahmā then? / Ten incarnations were yours to sport in ancient times, the Fish, the Tortoise, and the others."
They were restrained by Rudra, who came and said: "Quarreling is not fitting for you." / Viṣṇu acted just so, assuming those ten incarnations.

"I remember Viṣṇu, four-armed, holding the conch, mace, and sword, / clad in yellow garments, ever adorned with the Kaustubha jewel, / the sole lord of the universe, who grants liberation as soon as he is remembered."
Enraged by these words, the daitya commanded the daityas: / "Kill that wicked one by means of elephants, serpents, water, and fire!"
Prahlāda said: / "Viṣṇu is in the elephant, Viṣṇu is in the serpent, Viṣṇu is in the water, Viṣṇu is in the fire; / he abides in you, O daitya, and he abides in me; apart from Viṣṇu, even the host of daityas does not exist."
When, though being subjected to death, he met death nowhere, / Hiraṇyakaśipu's chest burned with the fire of wrath. / Then, placing his son before his face in order to discipline him,
he prepared to kill his son himself with harsh words: / "Fie on you! You praise Nārāyaṇa; if you praise my enemy again,
I will sever your head with my excellent sword as if plucking a flower! / I am Viṣṇu! I am Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra! Speak what is best!

17.18.m:
Forsaking your own father, whom else do you praise, boy?"
When the boy did not recite and did not praise his own father, / struck with a staff, Prahlāda was urged again by his teacher: / "Speak this one word, pupil; give me the fee due to the teacher,
so that my master may be pleased and give me abundant wealth."
Prahlāda said: / "Strike me first, teacher; [yet] I will obey your word: / I praise Viṣṇu, by whom the three worlds, with the moving and the unmoving,
were created, sustained, and brought to peace; may that Viṣṇu be pleased with me! / Brahmā is Viṣṇu, Hara is Viṣṇu, Indra, Vāyu, Yama, and Agni;
the principles beginning with nature, and the twenty-fifth, the Spirit— / he resides in the body of my father, in the body of my teacher, and in my body as well.
Knowing thus, how can I praise a vile man who is subject to death?"
The teacher said: / "Who is the lowest among men, O pupil, low from birth to death? / Why do you, facing death, not praise your father, [instead of] Hari, Hari?"

17.18.m:
Prahlāda said: / "While eating, lying down, traveling, in fever, spitting, or in battle, / one who does not utter the syllable 'Hari' at the time of death is the lowest of men. / In danger, in the royal court, in battle, in disease, during union with a woman, in the forest, / in weakness, or during renunciation, [and] at the time of death, dwelling on earth, / fools and the lowest of men remember their mother and father.
I have no mother, no father, nor do I have any kinsman. / Except for Hari, no one exists. Let whatever is deemed proper be done!"
Enraged by such words, the Daitya rose to kill [him]. / Then his mother came and stood before her son:
"Brothers, kinsmen, your sister says: 'Do not speak of Hari!' / I am your mother, here is your sister, your brothers, and your kin. / [Act] so that we, united together, may live for many days, my child."
Prahlāda said: / "Who is my mother? Who is my sister? Who are my brothers, and who is my father? / Listen to who my kin are, O mother, with whom I dwell forever.
